items.headline: Berlin-developed Ebola vaccine heads toward African trial
items.preview: Minapharm's Ebola vaccine candidate is advancing to clinical trials in Africa, supported by CEPI.
items.article:
The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) is providing Egyptian biopharmaceutical company Minapharm with up to $16.5 million to advance another vaccine candidate against Bundibugyo Ebola virus into clinical development. The candidate was developed by Minapharm’s Berlin-based subsidiary ProBioGen using its proprietary MVA-CR19 platform. A Phase I trial is planned in Africa, with the broader aim of helping the continent build the capacity to respond rapidly to emerging outbreaks.

Why this matters: The Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is becoming a stress test for global vaccine preparedness. The outbreak is not being caused by Zaire Ebola virus, for which the approved vaccine Ervebo is already available, but by the much rarer Bundibugyo Ebola virus. There is currently neither an approved vaccine nor a specific treatment for this virus. At the same time, case numbers in the DR Congo continue to rise exponentially.

items.headline: AstraZeneca, Ionis data spark debate about RNA drugs’ impact on deadly heart disease
items.preview: New trial results raise questions about the efficacy of RNA drugs in treating heart disease.
items.article:
Two years ago, Alnylam Pharmaceuticals presented study data showing that people with a deadly heart condition would live longer, and better avoid hospital stays, if they received a drug combination involving nucleic acid-based medicine it had developed. New study results published in the New England Journal of Medicine and presented at a medical meeting, however, raise questions about the impact drugs like Amvuttra have.

Why this matters: The trial enrolled more than 1,400 volunteers already on standard of care medications. After 140 weeks, investigators didn’t detect a statistically significant reduction in the risk of a cardiovascular event or death, which surprised investors and analysts and called into question how helpful it might be to use these silencing medications.

items.headline: What’s in Merck and Moderna’s cancer vaccine algorithm?
items.preview: Moderna and Merck's personalized cancer vaccine may hinge on a proprietary algorithm.
items.article:
Moderna and Merck’s personalized cancer vaccine could become the first approved medicine whose genetic instructions are essentially written by an algorithm. For each patient, software analyzes thousands of tumor mutations and chooses 34 neoantigens to encode into a bespoke mRNA vaccine.

Why this matters: Some skeptical investors think that perhaps the personalization isn’t necessary at all, and that mRNA itself primes tumors to respond better to Keytruda. Understanding the algorithm's role could be crucial for the future of personalized cancer treatments.

items.headline: Targeting METTL3/m6A/SOCS3 Reprograms Macrophages, Boosting Anti-PD-1 Therapy in Multiple Myeloma
items.preview: Research shows that reprogramming macrophages can enhance anti-PD-1 therapy in myeloma.
items.article:
Multiple myeloma may be vulnerable to an unexpected form of immune-system engineering: changing the behavior of the macrophages that surround the cancer. In a preclinical study, researchers report that restoring a molecule called SOCS3 can both restrain myeloma cells directly and transform tumor-associated macrophages into immune cells with a more inflammatory, cancer-fighting profile.

Why this matters: The findings help explain why checkpoint inhibitors have had more limited success in multiple myeloma. By altering macrophage polarization, the SOCS3 strategy may address one of the missing ingredients needed for an effective immune response.

items.headline: STRIPAK-associated greenbeard proteins DOC1 and DOC2 regulate MAK2 signaling and sexual development in Sordaria macrospora
items.preview: Study reveals the role of DOC proteins in fungal sexual development and signaling.
items.article:
Hyphal fusion and sexual development in filamentous fungi rely on coordinated signaling of numerous conserved nodes. Here, we used the homothallic ascomycete Sordaria macrospora to screen for putative protein interactors of the SmSTRIPAK complex. The deletion of SmDOC1 and SmDOC2 exhibited wild-type fertility and development, demonstrating non-redundant and mutually antagonistic roles.

Why this matters: These findings suggest the DOC1/2 proteins as a novel system that integrates STRIPAK and PR pathways, providing a possible mechanistic explanation for their non-additive deletion strain phenotypes.
